content.title: McNeese State brings 10-game win streak to Oklahoma City
content.text: The 12th-seeded Cowboys bring a 10-game winning streak and the nation’s fastest defensive pace into a first-round matchup against a fifth-seeded Vanderbilt team The McNeese State Cowboys arrive at the 2026 NCAA Tournament as a 12 seed riding one of the more impressive late-season runs in the field. The Cowboys have won 10 consecutive games, including a 76-59 victory over Stephen F. Austin in the Southland Conference Tournament final on Wednesday, and have not lost since February 2. Their 28-5 record and 19-3 conference mark reflect a program that has been one of the most consistent in its league all season. Vanderbilt enters as the fifth seed with a 26-8 record and four wins in its last five outings, the lone blemish being an 86-75 loss to Arkansas in the SEC Tournament title game on Sunday. The Commodores tied for fourth in the SEC regular-season standings at 11-7, a respectable finish in one of college basketball’s strongest conferences. The two programs have never met. Tipoff from the Paycom Center in Oklahoma City is scheduled for 3:15 p.m. Thursday on truTV. Vanderbilt opens as an 11.5-point favorite. What makes McNeese worth watching McNeese has been one of the more analytically interesting teams in the country this season regardless of conference. The Cowboys ranked first in the Southland in both offensive and defensive efficiency, and they have built their identity around pace, free throw generation and their ability to turn opponents’ possessions into quick scoring opportunities. Their style is defined by speed. McNeese ranks at or near the bottom nationally in defensive possession length, meaning the Cowboys push the pace relentlessly and force games into a rhythm that can be difficult for more methodically structured opponents to match. They ranked in the top 100 nationally in free throw rate, generating points at the line at a volume that reflects how aggressively they attack the basket. Larry Johnson figures to be their primary offensive engine in this matchup. The Cowboys will need him to generate early looks against a Vanderbilt defense that is structurally different from anything McNeese has faced in Southland play. What Vanderbilt brings to the floor The Commodores present a genuine challenge for the Cowboys’ preferred style. Vanderbilt’s roster is loaded with length in the frontcourt and a rotation of guards who are comfortable in an up-tempo setting, which means McNeese may not be able to dictate pace as effectively as it has against Southland opponents. Duke Miles leads the Vanderbilt offense and figures to be the Commodores’ most important player in this game. The supporting cast includes senior frontcourt pieces whose foul tendencies could become a factor as McNeese attacks the rim, potentially creating situations where rotation players see extended minutes and their own scoring opportunities increase. Vanderbilt head coach Mary Byington is conservative about playing key contributors who have picked up early fouls, which could create openings deeper in the rotation if McNeese’s free throw rate forces early foul trouble on Vanderbilt’s primary frontcourt players. How this game is likely to unfold The stylistic matchup points toward a higher-scoring game than Vanderbilt’s defensive identity might typically suggest. Both teams have players capable of generating offense in transition, McNeese by design and Vanderbilt by virtue of its guard rotation. The Cowboys will look to push tempo from the opening possession, and Vanderbilt’s guards have both the athleticism and the confidence to match that energy rather than slow it down. Where the game likely turns is the interior. Vanderbilt’s length gives the Commodores a real advantage on the glass, which matters because McNeese’s offense is predicated in part on offensive rebounding opportunities and second-chance points. If Vanderbilt cleans the glass effectively and limits McNeese’s second looks, the Cowboys’ path to covering the spread becomes considerably more difficult. McNeese has been the story of the Southland Conference for most of this season, and Today gives the Cowboys a national stage to show whether what they have built translates against a program with SEC credentials and a roster built for this moment.
